# Benchmark results

The tables below compare tsrs, TypeScript 7 (tsgo) and `bun check` on seventeen projects. CI updates them on each
benchmark publish. See [the methodology](README.md) for the commands, pinned projects, hardware and measurement details,
and [all recorded runs](results/) for other thread counts and instruction counts.

## Benchmark: tsrs vs tsgo 7.0.2 vs bun check

Time and peak memory to type-check each project (`-p <project> --noEmit`) on Depot CI `depot-ubuntu-24.04-16` (16 vCPU, 63 GB RAM, Linux x86_64, AMD EPYC 9R45 96-Core Processor). Median of 10 interleaved runs (3 for tsgo).

- **tsrs**: commit `3525a693e465`, PGO-optimized `dist` build, built like the npm release binaries.
- **tsgo**: npm `typescript@7.0.2`, the official Go compiler. tsrs ports a later 7.1-dev commit (`b85298b6`).
- **bun check**: Bun 1.4.4-canary.1+6c1eb067e.

Projects: vscode, xstate-main, webpack, mui-docs, Compiler, Compiler-Unions are from [microsoft/typescript-benchmarking](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-benchmarking), the suite the TypeScript team benchmarks tsgo on; the other 11 are large open-source applications.

### Default settings on 16 vCPUs

No thread flags: tsgo runs 4 checker threads; tsrs runs 16 (its default: all cores up to 16, then half the cores, at most 32; fewer on small projects); bun check runs one thread per core.

**Errors.** tsgo and tsrs report the same errors on 9 of 17 projects. The other 8 differ only because TypeScript changed between 7.0.2 and the 7.1-dev commit tsrs ports: `typescript@7.1.0-dev.20260930.4`, built from that commit, reports exactly tsrs's errors (tsgo / tsrs): vscode 359 / 371, webpack 848 / 840, supabase-studio 0 / 9, t3code-server 5 / 6, next-packages-next 6 / 5, next-root 441 / 438, nuxt 3 / 4, drizzle-orm 10845 / 10846. bun check, which follows TypeScript 7.0 like tsgo, differs from tsgo on webpack (837 errors, tsgo 848).

Rows are sorted by speedup over tsgo. Wall time is the process's wall clock; peak memory is its maximum resident set size. Bold marks a win over tsgo of at least 5x in time or 4x in memory.

Shared CI machines vary by a few percent between runs of the same code; the single-threaded instruction counts in `bench/results/` are the exact measure. Date: 2026-10-11 14:57 UTC. tsrs commit: `3525a693e465`. Method: [benchmark methodology](https://github.com/maschwenk/tsrs/blob/main/bench/README.md).

## Large-project chart snapshot

The [README chart](large-projects.svg) is a static snapshot of the **2026-10-11 14:32 UTC** CI benchmark at
`tsrs` commit `b8bdd76bf789`, using each project's `wide` results. It shows **median wall time and peak RSS**
at default settings. CI does not regenerate the SVG.

[Raw measurements](results/2026-10-11-b8bdd76bf789.json) ·
[All settings](results/2026-10-11-b8bdd76bf789.md) · [Methodology](README.md#what-is-measured)

- **Machine:** Depot `depot-ubuntu-24.04-16`, 16 vCPUs, 63 GiB RAM, Linux x86_64, AMD EPYC 9R45.
- **TypeScript:** `typescript@7.0.2`, the native Go compiler, 4 checker threads, median of 3 runs.
- **`tsrs`:** `0.13.0-ts7.1.0-dev.20260929`, PGO-optimized `dist` build with BOLT, built like the npm release;
  up to 16 checker threads, median of 10 runs. Rust compiler: `rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28)`.

The harness interleaves compiler runs, measures process wall time and maximum resident set size, and disables
incremental compilation. Both native binaries run directly, without a Node launcher.

| Repository and measured project | Files | Time: TypeScript 7 → `tsrs` | Peak memory: TypeScript 7 → `tsrs` | Speedup | Less peak memory |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [VS Code](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode), `src` | 10,427 | 10.96 s → 0.86 s | 7.63 GiB → 2.09 GiB | **12.7×** | **73%** |
| [T3 Code](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code), `apps/server` | 2,945 | 13.66 s → 1.37 s | 6.19 GiB → 2.14 GiB | **10.0×** | **65%** |
| [MUI docs](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), `docs` | 16,766 | 12.24 s → 0.86 s | 7.50 GiB → 1.60 GiB | **14.2×** | **79%** |

File counts are `tsrs`'s compiled program files, including dependencies and TypeScript libraries, for the named
project within each repository. TypeScript 7.0.2 loads 2,941 files for T3 Code; `tsrs` loads 2,945. The other two
counts agree. Ratios use unrounded medians; GiB means bytes divided by 2³⁰. All three rows share a 0–16 second
time scale and a 0–8 GiB memory scale.

The compilers follow different TypeScript revisions: `tsrs` ports 7.1-dev commit `b85298b6a81f`. For VS Code and
T3 Code, the matching nightly `typescript@7.1.0-dev.20260930.4` reports exactly `tsrs`'s diagnostic locations and
codes. All timed runs completed; VS Code and T3 Code contain diagnostics, so these are completed type checks
rather than error-free builds.

| Project | Pinned repository commit | Diagnostics: TypeScript 7.0.2 → `tsrs` |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| VS Code | `9cf0128b9822` | 359 → 371 |
| T3 Code | `9bd1d8009a6b` | 5 → 6 |
| MUI docs | `6780195595c1` | 0 → 0 |

## Historical comparison on 64 vCPUs

On 2026-10-07, type-checking vscode (10,427 files) on a 64-core Linux machine, each tool with its default settings, averaged over 20
runs ([source](results/compare/2026-10-07-ae33f10b1b8b-64t.md)):

| | time | peak memory |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| tsc 7 (tsgo 7.0.2) | 9.79 s | 7.52 GiB |
| `bun check` (Bun 1.4.3 canary) | 0.87 s | 2.86 GiB |
| **tsrs** | **0.53 s** | **2.64 GiB** |

### Against bun check at equal thread counts

The tools pick different thread counts by default, so here each one gets the same number (vscode, 64-core machine, 20
runs each):

| threads | tsgo 7.0.2 | tsrs | `bun check` |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 9.75 s, 7.43 GiB | 2.43 s, 1.83 GiB | 4.57 s, 1.46 GiB |
| 8 | 6.13 s, 7.99 GiB | 1.35 s, 1.97 GiB | 2.47 s, 1.60 GiB |
| 16 | 4.54 s, 8.67 GiB | 0.81 s, 2.13 GiB | 1.49 s, 1.85 GiB |
| 64 | 4.01 s, 11.58 GiB | 0.44 s, 3.06 GiB | 0.87 s, 2.86 GiB |

tsrs is about 1.9x faster at every thread count; tsrs uses 7-25% more memory. `bun check` follows TypeScript
7.0 and tsrs follows 7.1-dev, so their error counts can differ slightly; each matches its own reference exactly.

[Benchmark methodology](README.md) explains how everything is measured and how to rerun it. The published numbers
use the PGO-optimized release build, which is 7-14% faster than a plain `cargo build --release`.
